title: JPMorgan's JPM Coin Shows Zero Supply on Ethereum (ETH) After Oct. 19 Launch - Cryptonews.net
content: JPMorgan's deposit token has been live on Ethereum ($ETH) since Oct. 19, and the contract data so far reads a flat zero. As of Oct. 22, the Ethereum deployment of JPM Coin (JPMD) showed zero circulating supply and zero recorded transfers, with exactly one allowlisted address registered in the verified smart contract. The bank, whose shares trade under JPMorgan (JPM), opened the token to approved institutional clients on the network that day, extending a rollout that began in November 2025 on Base, Coinbase's Layer 2 network. The Base contract tells a quieter version of the same story: about 1,001,000 tokens held across two addresses, unchanged since Nov. 20, 2025. JPM Coin is a tokenized claim on dollar deposits held at the bank, and its structure differs from an open stablecoin: the contract sits on a public blockchain, but only approved customer addresses can receive the token. Sentora, the on-chain research firm behind the review published Oct. 23, notes that an address count measures registered addresses, not customers or actual users, and that a standing supply figure cannot capture payments where issuance and redemption happen within the same day. In plain terms, supply is the amount of a token outstanding at a given moment, so the zero balance describes the Ethereum ($ETH) contract's state on Oct. 22 rather than everything JPM Coin does across networks. The unchanged Base balance also does not rule out earlier transfers, since the review reports a snapshot rather than a full transfer history for that network. The Oct. 19 announcement cited Ethereum's tokenized asset and liquidity base as the reason for expansion, but an announcement and actual issuance are separate stages, and JPMorgan has not disclosed issuance or transaction volumes for the new deployment. The launch landed while Ethereum price discussion this week has centered on institutional flows rather than new rails. Sentora's published research adds the second data point, and this one shows movement. Its contract-level analysis put $400 million in redemptions on the Ethereum ($ETH) deployment of JLTXX, a tokenized money market fund from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, across Oct. 21 and Oct. 22. Over the same two days, the fund's Solana deployment climbed from effectively zero to $450 million. The pairing is suggestive rather than conclusive: one figure is a redemption flow, the other a standing deployment size, and the data does not tie individual investors to both sides of the move. The product context arrived on Oct. 22, when the asset manager announced that JLTXX and its My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) were open to qualified U.S. investors on Solana, with subscriptions and redemptions handled through the firm's Morgan Money platform. JLTXX is described in that announcement as a U.S. registered government money market fund built to support stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. “Our clients operate across more than one network, and their liquidity should too,” said Paul Przybylski, who leads product, digital and tokenized assets at the firm. MONY, a private placement launched in December 2025, carries a $1 million minimum, fees of 16 basis points, and a portfolio of U.S. Treasury securities and Treasury-backed repurchase agreements targeting a $1 net asset value per share outside Rule 2a-7. Investors need their own blockchain addresses to hold the tokens, peer-to-peer transfers are restricted to clients, and official shareholder records stay off-chain with SS&C as transfer agent. JPMorgan's materials also note that interests in the funds are not bank accounts and carry no Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insurance. The same briefing found no live on-chain integration connecting JPM Coin with the bank's funds or decentralized finance protocols. The two records read together sketch where institutional usage of Ethereum actually stands. On Sentora's published research, the primary document behind both stories, the newest institutional rail is live in name only four days after its announcement, while the fund flow data shows Ethereum holding a large tokenized money market footprint but ceding its fastest-growing leg to Solana. Neither point is, by itself, a verdict on Ethereum adoption: allowlisted deployments start slowly by design, and same-day issue-and-redeem payments would leave no trace in a standing balance. The markers worth tracking are specific: the first non-zero issuance or transfer on the Ethereum JPMD contract, and whether JLTXX's Ethereum deployment stabilizes once the Oct. 21–22 redemption window is behind it. Broader market pressure is a separate variable: spot ETF products logged a $110.6 million net outflow on Oct. 22, and the chart sits near the $2,300 support zone ahead of the Federal Reserve decision.

title: JPMorgan Expands Tokenized Money Market Funds To Solana - TradingView
content: TL;DR: J.P. Morgan Asset Management says qualified U.S. investors can now access MONY and JLTXX tokenized money market funds on Solana through its Morgan Money platform. J.P. Morgan Asset Management is bringing two of its tokenized money market funds to Solana, extending a traditional cash-management business across another public blockchain. In an announcement Thursday, the investment manager said qualified U.S. investors can now access My OnChain Net Yield Fund, known as MONY, and the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity–Token Money Market Fund, JLTXX, on Solana through its Morgan Money platform. Investors can subscribe and redeem through that institutional interface and receive balances represented at blockchain addresses. The two products are not identical forms of digital cash. MONY is a private placement offered under Rule 506(c), with eligibility restrictions for qualifying investors. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund structured to serve cash management needs, including those of stablecoin issuers. Both represent fund interests rather than ordinary deposit balances. J.P. Morgan's disclosures make clear that the funds are not bank accounts or FDIC-insured deposits, and that even products seeking a stable $1 share value can lose money. That difference is easy to overlook when a token moves through a wallet interface. The blockchain record can make ownership and transfers more programmable; it does not change the underlying fund's investment objectives, regulatory status or redemption restrictions. Institutions experimenting with tokenized assets increasingly operate across more than one chain. A fund that can be subscribed into on multiple networks may be more useful as a liquidity-management instrument, particularly when portfolio and treasury teams hold digital balances in different environments. J.P. Morgan says adding Solana is intended to let clients access the same fund strategies across the networks where they operate. It is a distribution and settlement expansion, not the creation of two wholly new investment strategies. The bank's Morgan Money platform remains central to the customer experience. That is significant because professional investors need controls that go beyond seeing a token balance, including eligibility screening, reporting, fund documents and predictable subscriptions and redemptions. The company published Solana token addresses for both products, but copying a token identifier from social media is not a substitute for using the manager's verified onboarding channel. Token impersonation and lookalike assets remain a risk in on-chain markets. For Solana, the listing adds another institutional financial product beyond speculative trading. For J.P. Morgan, it tests whether a familiar regulated fund structure can retain its governance while using a wider set of blockchain rails. Actual institutional adoption and transaction volumes, not the announcement alone, will show the importance of that change. Source: www.prnewswire.com original announcement or data. title: JPM Coin has zero Ethereum supply after launch, Sentora says - Crypto News
content: JPMorgan’s JPM Coin has recorded zero supply and zero transfers on Ethereum in a contract review by Sentora, days after the bank announced the deposit token’s arrival on the network. Sentora said its review found exactly one allowlisted address in the verified Ethereum contract, while the token’s Base deployment held roughly $1 million across two addresses, unchanged since November 2025. The research firm’s findings cover the deposit token and separate movements in J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s tokenized liquidity fund. Its briefing reported $400 million in JLTXX redemptions on Ethereum across Oct. 21–22, alongside a rise in the fund’s Solana deployment from near zero to $450 million. Sentora attributed those figures to its contract-level analysis. The timing does not establish that the same investors redeemed on Ethereum and subscribed on Solana, and the briefing did not identify transactions connecting the two movements. JPMorgan brought JPM Coin, which carries the ticker JPMD, to Ethereum for approved institutional clients on Oct. 19. As crypto.news previously reported, the bank’s Ethereum deposit token launch followed its November 2025 rollout on Base. The deposit token represents U.S. dollar deposits held at JPMorgan. The launch coverage described institutional payments, securities settlement, and collateral payments as intended uses, with access restricted to approved customers despite the use of a public blockchain. Sentora’s subsequent review reported no issued supply or transfers in the Ethereum contract it examined. Its Base findings described an unchanged supply balance, with holdings concentrated in two addresses. An unchanged supply figure does not, by itself, establish whether transfers occurred during that period. Sentora’s briefing expressly reported zero transfers for Ethereum but did not provide an equivalent historical transfer count for Base. The firm further said it had found no live on-chain integration between JPM Coin and the bank’s money market funds or decentralized finance protocols. Its statement concerned the integrations visible in its review, without documenting every potential institutional arrangement. Sentora reported that JLTXX’s Ethereum deployment recorded $400 million in redemptions across Oct. 21–22. Over the same period, its briefing placed the Solana deployment at $450 million after starting near zero. The figures describe different measures across two networks. One is a redemption total, while the other is the reported size of a deployment after its growth. They do not establish an exact dollar-for-dollar migration. J.P. Morgan Asset Management announced on Oct. 22 that JLTXX and its My OnChain Net Yield Fund, known as MONY, were available to qualified U.S. investors on Solana. Investors can access the two tokenized funds through Morgan Money, which handles subscriptions and redemptions and delivers token balances to blockchain addresses. “Our clients operate across more than one network, and their liquidity should too,” said Paul Przybylski, the asset manager’s global head of product, digital and tokenized assets. The company’s announcement identifies JLTXX as a U.S. registered government money market fund designed to support stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. MONY is a separate private placement fund launched in December 2025. The release does not disclose assets held on Solana for either product. JPMorgan’s MONY FAQ lists a $1 million initial investment minimum and fees of 16 basis points. The document describes a British Virgin Islands private placement vehicle, with access subject to anti-money laundering and know-your-customer checks. The FAQ says MONY invests in U.S. Treasury securities and Treasury-backed repurchase agreements, seeking a stable net asset value of $1 per share. Although its guidelines follow those applicable to government money market funds, the private vehicle is not subject to Rule 2a-7. JPMorgan identifies SS&C as MONY’s transfer agent and says the official shareholder records remain off-chain. Investors need their own blockchain addresses to hold tokens, while peer-to-peer transfers are restricted to clients. The Oct. 22 launch announcement warns that investments in the funds are not bank accounts and are not insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. JPMorgan says the funds seek to preserve a $1 share value but cannot guarantee it. A separate institutional transaction involved BNY’s tokenized Treasury repo deal with Citadel Securities, announced on Oct. 13. BNY said Citadel Securities purchased a two-year U.S. Treasury note through the bank on Tradeweb. A tokenized representation of the security settled within minutes on BNY’s private digital ledger before Citadel Securities pledged it as collateral in an overnight triparty repurchase agreement. BNY supplied cash against the security and described the transaction as the first use of tokenized assets on a major triparty repo platform. Its announcement documented trade execution, settlement and financing within the same workflow. The bank said it plans to introduce further digital cash and tokenized deposit services. BNY expects to expand operating hours for its traditional settlement platforms covering Fed-eligible securities and U.S. triparty transactions into European and Asian trading hours next year. title: Rockefeller Lands $4.8M J.P. Morgan Team in Houston, UBS Duo in Ohio - AdvisorHub
content: Rockefeller Global Family Office has hired a J.P. Morgan Wealth Management team in Houston that oversaw $700 million in client assets and a UBS Wealth Management USA team in Columbus, Ohio, that oversaw $350 million, according to a source familiar with the moves. The Houston team, Sage Wealth Partners, is led by Christopher D. Sheets and Forrest R. Green and produced $4.8 million in annual revenue, according to the source. At J.P. Morgan Advisors, the pair worked with a third partner, T. Scott Holstead, as SGH Group. Holstead, a founding member of the Houston wealth office, remained with J.P. Morgan, but the other nine members of the team—including Sheets’ son Cameron—made the move, a second source said. Sheets and Green joined J.P. Morgan in 2018. They began their advisory careers at Bernstein Private Wealth Management in 2002 and 2004, respectively, according to registration records. The UBS team, Shea Wealth Partners, is led by Andrea M. Shea and her son, Martin E. Shea, who produced $2.5 million in annual revenue, the source said. The four-person team worked out of UBS offices in the Columbus suburb of Upper Arlington and near Cleveland in Pepper Pike, Ohio, according to its UBS website, which was no longer online Friday afternoon. Andrea Shea joined UBS in 2009 after four years with Morgan Stanley predecessor Smith Barney, according to registration records. She began her career in 1998 and was registered with three brokerages through 2000. Martin Shea joined her at UBS in 2022. Spokespeople for J.P. Morgan and UBS did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Rockefeller opened an office in Columbus in August with Jones Wealth Partners, a team from Merrill Lynch, and also has offices in Cincinnati and Cleveland, the firm said at the time. In Houston, Rockefeller in April snagged a Merrill Lynch team producing $14 million in annual revenue. Rockefeller Capital Management, the parent of Rockefeller Global Family Office, reported overseeing $237 billion in client assets at the end of August. Earlier this month, the firm hired a $1.2 billion Truist team that joined an office in Naples, Florida, established five months earlier with the addition of a billion-dollar Morgan Stanley team. J.P. Morgan Advisors, the bank’s traditional brokerage unit, has around 600 advisors. Last week, two of the unit’s largest teams, led by Phil Scott and Jim Atwood, left to launch their own RIA with $18.6 billion in client assets and $130 million in combined annual revenue. J.P. Morgan Wealth Management had 6,433 advisors, including those in Chase bank branches, at the end of September, up 7% from a year earlier, according to its earnings report. UBS’s Americas wealth unit had 5,644 advisors at the end of June, down 2.2% from a year earlier. At least 54 teams with $51.8 billion in client assets left UBS for rivals in 2025, and at least 27 teams with $28 billion departed in the first half of this year. Shawn L. Bernhard had spent less than 18 months at Raymond James after a lengthy career at UBS.

Santiago-listed Chilean pulp and paper group Empresas CMPC has agreed to sell 60,000 hectares (148,263 acres) of radiata pine forestland, or approximately 5 percent of its total timberland holdings, to J.P. Morgan Natural Capital for US$365 million. The transaction, which was executed through CMPC subsidiary Forestal Mininco and J.P. Morgan Natural Capital subsidiary Bosques San Pedro SpA, also includes a long-term timber supply agreement through which CMPC will purchase timber from the assets being transferred as raw materials for its cardboard operations. “This transaction is part of our long-term asset management strategy announced at the end of last year. It was a competitive process, aimed at strengthening our focus on our core businesses and moving towards greater levels of efficiency and competitiveness,” stated Sebastián Moraga, vice president of finance and administration, CMPC. Chile’s forestry sector is one of the most established and commercially developed in Latin America, supported by favorable growing conditions, a well-developed timber processing industry, and access to international export markets. The country’s temperate climate, productive soils, and extensive plantation resources provide favorable conditions for fast-growing commercial species, particularly radiata pine and eucalyptus. Demand for sustainable building materials, wood-based packaging, pulp, and other bio-based products are poised to create additional growth opportunities as industries seek alternatives to fossil-based and carbon-intensive materials. And for institutional investors, commercial plantations can provide recurring revenue through planned harvest cycles, while well-managed timberland may appreciate in value as trees mature and land-use opportunities evolve. Beyond traditional timber revenues, the wider South American timberland market offers opportunities to create additional value through reforestation, biodiversity protection, and carbon-credit projects by acquiring underutilized or degraded land, improving forest productivity, and investing in better genetics and management practices such as integrating timber production with conservation efforts. Furthermore, compared with many Northern Hemisphere forestry markets, selected Latin American regions can offer shorter rotations and competitive production costs. title: Norwegian Cruise Line cut to underweight as yield recovery faces risks—J.P. Morgan - TradingView
content: Like the rest of the sector and other industries heavily dependent on fuel, Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings NCLH faces pressure on its bottom line that will be only partially offset by higher passenger spending. Simply put, operating expenses will grow faster than the market anticipates, potentially putting additional pressure on Norwegian’s profitability. According to J.P. Morgan’s Matthew Boss, Norwegian Cruise Line’s NCLH third quarter performance could be better than expected, but the cruise operator’s underlying revenue performance remains challenged. With revenue likely to disappoint in the first half of 2027, Boss downgrades Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings NCLH to Underweight from Neutral and trims his price target by 15% to $11, implying a 30% downside to Thursday’s closing price. Boss sees Norwegian’s NCLH net yield declining by 6.5% versus Wall Street’s -6.2% estimate, and costs excluding fuel to be up 1.1% compared to the street estimate of up 0.9%, resulting in a loss of $0.12 per share, a penny wider than the consensus estimate. The difference is blamed on higher fuel costs, which Boss expects will be more significant than either the company or Wall Street is forecasting. While the second half of 2027 should see improving yields (+3.2% versus -5.3% in Q1 and -1.6% in Q2), the rebound assumes easing geopolitical tensions in Europe, given that 85% of Norwegian’s European cruise itineraries are booked by U.S. passengers, the highest proportion within the industry. The downgrade coupled with the upward trend in oil futures is driving down shares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings NCLH along with peers Royal Caribbean RCL and Carnival Corp CCL. title: Diversifying against the big risks JP Morgan sees today - Wealth Professional
content: Jared Gross explains how alternatives can stack up against growth, inflation, and concentration risks Each month at WP we focus on a particular topic of interest to advisors. This October we’re focusing on private assets and alternatives. Investors are aware of the big risks that could be facing their portfolios, on the broadest level. They know that a growth shock can come, that inflation can rear its head, or that markets can become too concentrated and correct. What they don’t know is when those risks will come and the magnitude of their impact on portfolios. That’s why investors follow Harry Markowitz to “the only free lunch in investing”: diversification. In the low inflation decades that preceded the 2020s, the 60/40 formula of equities and bonds appeared like it was enough diversification to work. Today, however, new risks are apparent even if their timing and magnitude remain unclear. Those risks should prompt investors and advisors to question how they will diversify. Jared Gross, Managing Director and Head of Institutional Portfolio Strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset Management outlined the state of growth, inflation, and concentration risk as he sees them. While growth risks are present, he stressed the increasing importance of controlling for inflation and concentration risks in portfolios today. He emphasized how the dynamics between those sets of risk has changed and outlined how alternatives as a broad asset class can help diversify against those risks. “When you think about risks that you want to diversify, there is a classic adage in the markets that you diversify the risks you do not know, you hedge the risks you do know,” Gross says. “And I think what that really means to most investors in practice is we understand that there are certain risks that show up at some point in time. We don’t know when. We don’t know to what magnitude. But they have the potential to cause significant damage to the value of a portfolio.” Inflation remains a core risk for investors today, as recent bond volatility demonstrates. However, Gross notes that the surprise of a risk like inflation serves to amplify its magnitude. Unlike 2022, inflation is not as surprising as it once was, making the risk somewhat more muted. Nevertheless, for investors seeking to manage inflation risk, Gross explains that there have been some historic asset classes designed to protect against inflation. Namely inflation-linked bonds and cash instruments which can operate in a floating rate structure. However, he says that it’s difficult for investors to hold enough of these instruments to form an effective hedge over the long-term, as their typically low return profile means the investor ends up underperforming return targets. While direct inflation hedges have the drawback of dampening long-term returns, Gross says that many investors have simply acknowledged that out-earning inflation in the long-term is the best way to manage that risk. That has traditionally meant an equity allocation, with the view that corporate earnings will be tied to GDP growth and therefore exceed inflation. However, the issue of concentration risk poses some challenges to a pure equity inflation hedge today. Gross says that certain real assets should be viewed favourably in this light. Real estate, infrastructure, transportation, and even some commodities like timber can produce long-term returns that meet client expectations, while showing significant resilience in the face of inflation. The other risk being identified in headlines and op-eds is the growing market concentration in a single investable theme: artificial intelligence. US equity markets have become highly concentrated in AI-related stocks, with nine of the top ten names on the S&P 500 connected directly to the theme. Those mega-cap AI and tech stocks now represent roughly 40 per cent of the benchmark, which might give some investors pause. Gross caveats that point by noting that the big tech names on the S&P 500 represent roughly 40 per cent of corporate earnings as well, making their concentration somewhat more ‘earned’ than the case of the revenue negative names that typified the dot com bubble. Nevertheless, there is a risk that those large companies may face disruption and that the passive investing momentum that has played a role in their performance might reverse. AI concentration also now extends beyond equities. Many of the AI ‘hyperscalers’ have issued a significant amount of debt, causing investment grade credit indices to carry a hefty weighting to AI. Because the AI data center buildout narrative is as much about land, energy, and construction it has become as much an infrastructure play as a technology theme. Diversifying from this theme involves both hedging against AI concentration entirely and diversifying the kinds of AI exposure that a portfolio carries. If momentum in AI reverses, Gross believes that actively managed value and quality strategies might offer some advantages. Looking at the alternatives space, he identified areas that now carry some connection to AI and sectors that are more insulated from the theme, arguing that investors may want to consider a combination of differentiated AI exposure and wholly non-exposed assets. Closed-end infrastructure funds, Gross says, can carry a high degree of exposure to AI data center construction. That’s because modern data centers function as infrastructure more than pure real estate, with a high degree of maintenance required and expensive internal components typically being built on cheap and widely available land near power generation. Regulated power delivery also offers an interesting way to play the AI theme, Gross notes, with some of those utilities with excess power in a strong position to charge a premium to data centers and reinvest that additional revenue in further generation. For investors who want to remove AI exposure from parts of their portfolio, Gross suggests that core real estate offers less than one per cent exposure to data centers. Government bonds, as well, have recently demonstrated negative correlation against US equities, making them a useful diversifier. For advisors who want to find differentiated ways to manage both inflation and concentration risk, and are considering alternatives, Gross emphasizes the importance of manager selection and vetting in their process. “The basic rule with alternatives is manager selection and individual fund performance is a much greater driver of outcomes than public market strategies where the market beta is the dominant factor that drives outcomes. And that’s both a risk, but it also means that a well-chosen strategy in any category can navigate this market environment successfully,” Gross says. “I do think strategies that are lower in the risk spectrum and/or have very low AI content are a useful hedge or place of greater safety in the event something goes wrong. And those don’t have to be low-returning investments.”

This JPMorgan announcement strengthens Solana's position in institutional finance. The JPMorgan Solana move covers two products with different investment structures. title: Credit markets look for AI’s weak links - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has hit turbulence over the past few weeks. AI-related stocks have fallen much more sharply than the broader market as investors reconsider the financing costs of building data centers, buying chips and supplying the electricity needed to run them. Still, investors have seen rotations out of AI before. What makes this episode different is the simultaneous action in credit markets. The cost of insuring the debt of several AI-linked companies has reached record levels as the sector grows more reliant on debt financing. But rather than a blanket vote against the ecosystem, the rising cost of default protection reflects a targeted reassessment of repayment risk. In other words, credit markets are taking a hard look at the AI build-out and asking who can afford to keep at it. Credit default swaps (CDS) act like insurance on a company’s debt. CDS buyers pay a recurring premium and, if the borrower experiences a major credit event, such as bankruptcy or failure to pay, the buyer will receive a large payout. The premium is quoted in basis points. A CDS spread of 100 basis points broadly means that insuring $10 million of debt costs $100,000 per year. At 1,000 basis points, the annual cost rises to roughly $1 million.1 Credit default swaps can provide a measure of market sentiment. A wider CDS spread does not necessarily signal an expected failure. It can also reflect greater hedging demand, heavy debt issuance or uncertainty about future financing. The level, speed and confirmation from other markets help distinguish routine insurance from genuine distress. Credit spreads have widened over the past month, but technology-related borrowers have moved much more sharply than the broader investment grade market. The spread between the two has spiked higher than even during the tech-driven downturn of 2022. Going one level deeper, AI-related CDS have risen even more rapidly in the past month, but not all in parallel. For large, cash-generative AI leaders, five-year CDS spreads range from 50–120 basis points. These are elevated levels for companies with strong balance sheets, but they still look more like the price of portfolio insurance than a prediction of financial distress. These companies still have far lower leverage and higher interest coverage ratios than the average investment grade borrower. The picture changes as debt becomes more important to the business model. Default protection on some established investment grade infrastructure borrowers has climbed toward 300 basis points. That represents a meaningful reassessment of credit risk. At the weak end of the spectrum, one financing-dependent AI infrastructure borrower has taken on tens of billions of dollars in debt and other obligations. Its five-year CDS shot up to 1,100 basis points this week, so insuring $10 million of its debt would cost more than $1 million per year. Pricing at these levels implies near or above a 50% probability of default over five years, up from below 30% a year ago. That is not a forecast, but it is difficult to dismiss.2 Put together, investors are demanding roughly 10 times as much to insure the weakest AI borrower as the strongest companies in the ecosystem. Yet broad investment grade protection remains comparatively contained. If markets were losing confidence in corporate balance sheets generally, that would not be the case. The concern is confined to business models that require debt markets to remain open while spending stays high and cash flow remains limited. Lehman Brothers’ CDS averaged less than 100 basis points in the third quarter of 2007. By mid-September 2008, they had risen to over 1,400 and the firm had filed for bankruptcy. CDS did not predict the exact moment when Lehman would run out of options. But the steady rise in protection costs, reinforced by falling bond and equity prices and mounting funding pressure, clearly showed that the market was losing confidence in the firm’s ability to pay its debts. Not every warning ends the same way. In 2005, default protection on a major U.S. automaker rose sharply ahead of its downgrade to high yield. The company’s financial pressure was real, but it raised liquidity, restructured and avoided bankruptcy. That is how investors can view CDS today—as warning lights rather than countdown clocks. As long as broad investment grade spreads remain contained, and stronger borrowers retain access to capital, stress among the riskiest issuers is unlikely to derail the broader AI build-out. However, the AI label alone is no longer enough to reassure lenders. Companies must show that they can finance investment, service their debt and eventually turn spending into cash flow. Their 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions predict a 10% annual return for Bitcoin over the next 10 to 15 years. This outpaces their projections for U.S. large-cap stocks at 7.5% and U.S. REITs at 8.2%. However, Bitcoin carries high risk, with estimated annual volatility of 55%. Investors who typically use a 60/40 mix of stocks and bonds may question whether their portfolio lacks diversity. Some may take bold steps; for instance, a recent Reddit post on r/wallstreetbets shared a user’s experience of investing almost all their liquid assets in Bitcoin and Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR), the largest corporate Bitcoin holder, which drew significant attention. Remember, the 10% return averages over many years. It doesn’t indicate where Bitcoin’s price will be in the coming year, and this forecast could include years of substantial losses. Bitcoin’s significant volatility plays a more critical role in shaping your investment outcome than its potential 10% return. How much Bitcoin you hold in your portfolio determines how much a significant downturn can affect your overall investment. A 50% drop in Bitcoin’s price will impact your portfolio based on your Bitcoin allocation. Here’s how Bitcoin allocations can affect your portfolio during a drop: Beyond the risk of drastic price drops, Bitcoin can also swing wildly in shorter time frames. For instance, while Bitcoin surged about 31% over the past 90 days, it remains 22% lower than it was a year ago. Excluding Bitcoin altogether eliminates the 55% volatility, but it also forgoes the potential for higher returns. This strategy may suit individuals nearing retirement or those who would panic and sell after a significant drop. A 1% or 5% allocation with regular rebalancing lets you benefit from Bitcoin’s upside while reducing the potential damage of a crash. For example, if your 5% Bitcoin investment doubles while your other investments stay the same, your Bitcoin slice would grow to about 9.5% of your portfolio. Rebalancing can help lock in gains by selling some Bitcoin to return to your original 5% allocation. This rebalancing strategy also works well after a price drop, as it lets you maintain your desired allocation without letting your Bitcoin exposure dwindle to almost nothing. Keep in mind the tax implications: selling Bitcoin in a taxable account may trigger capital gains tax, while a spot Bitcoin ETF in an IRA can be adjusted without immediate tax consequences. By contrast, a 10% Bitcoin allocation or more—especially through a leveraged investment like Strategy—might not be advisable for most households. With a 10% Bitcoin allocation, a 50% drop reduces the entire portfolio’s value by 5%. Furthermore, swapping Bitcoin for a leverage-dependent asset amplifies risk, which is something only investors with a long time horizon, solid cash reserves, and the ability to endure downturns should consider. For most investors interested in Bitcoin, aiming for a smaller allocation—around 1% or 5%—is generally more sensible. This conservatively sized investment accounts for the high volatility while aligning with the potential for favorable returns. This approach suits individuals who have already secured their emergency fund and retirement savings and can hold through significant fluctuations without selling their Bitcoin. Successful investing depends on sizing your position based on volatility rather than chasing headlines about potential returns. Many investors jump in after big gains and sell into losses, ultimately doing worse than steady investors. It helps to set a rebalancing rule, such as reviewing your allocation once a year. If J.P. J.P. Morgan examined global banks' exposure to CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) following a decline in the AI cloud infrastructure provider's shares and bonds. The market movements occurred amid growing scrutiny of the borrowing required to finance the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. CoreWeave has accumulated approximately $50 billion in debt while developing computing capacity for major technology customers. Last week, the yield on its bonds due in 2031 approached 16%, while the cost of credit default protection rose to around 1,000 basis points. The developments prompted questions about whether financial pressure at AI infrastructure companies could create risks for the banks providing their funding. According to J.P. Morgan, large US investment banks and Japan's MUFG could each have between $1 billion and $3 billion in exposure to CoreWeave. Most other European and Asian institutions are estimated to have exposures below $500 million. The figures are based on simplified assumptions because banks do not provide comprehensive disclosures about their lending and investment exposure to the AI infrastructure sector. J.P. Morgan therefore cautioned that the estimates should not be treated as precise measures of individual banks' positions. J.P. Morgan identified the structure of CoreWeave's borrowing arrangements as an important factor in assessing lenders' risks. Much of the financing consists of delayed draw term loans, under which committed funds are released in stages as projects achieve agreed milestones. These arrangements are largely managed through special-purpose vehicles and are supported by security arrangements linked to the financed assets. CoreWeave has approximately $24 billion in committed delayed draw term loans, including $15 billion already drawn and $9 billion not yet utilised. J.P. Morgan analysts led by Kian Abouhossein said the banks' exposures were well managed and secured. The brokerage's assessment suggests that the structure of the financing may limit direct lender risks, although it does not remove the possibility of losses. CoreWeave's business requires substantial spending on data centres and computing equipment before the full revenue associated with customer contracts is received. The company has secured agreements worth tens of billions of dollars with major technology businesses, but its infrastructure expansion continues to require external capital. J.P. Morgan identified the timing difference between upfront investment and future customer payments as a central financial risk. The brokerage expects CoreWeave's free cash flow to remain negative until 2030. This forecast indicates that the company may continue to require financing to support its capital expenditure and operating requirements. J.P. Morgan maintains an overweight rating on CoreWeave, with a price target of $125 for the end of 2027. The brokerage's assessment of the banking sector focuses on the direct credit exposure of lenders rather than solely on movements in CoreWeave's share price or bond yields. Although the company's debt securities have experienced significant selling pressure, J.P. Morgan estimates that most global banks have relatively limited exposure. The analysis also highlights the uncertainty surrounding broader AI infrastructure financing, particularly because banks provide limited disclosure about their involvement in the sector. For lenders, the principal considerations remain the security supporting individual loans, the progress of financed projects and the ability of borrowers to generate sufficient cash flow over time. title: JPM Coin Ethereum Launch 2026: Not a Stablecoin, and Why - Memeburn
content: JPM Coin is now live on Ethereum, the blockchain where apps hold almost $50 billion in crypto, for JPMorgan's institutional clients. You'll see how a bank deposit token differs from stablecoins like USDT, why JPMorgan picked a public network, and how this sets up a fight over who issues digital dollars. JPMorgan, the biggest bank in the US, has launched JPM Coin on Ethereum, the public blockchain where crypto apps hold almost $50 billion in assets. JPM Coin is a digital version of dollars sitting in JPMorgan bank accounts, and moving it onto the same open network that stablecoins like USDT and USDC dominate shows banks are no longer watching crypto from the sidelines. Here’s what JPMorgan actually launched, how it differs from a stablecoin, and what it could mean for the future of digital money. 20% Lifetime Discount on Trading Fees Code Valid: October 2026 JPM Coin, which trades under the ticker JPMD, is run by Kinexys, JPMorgan’s blockchain business. Each token stands for one US dollar held as a deposit at the bank. It first launched in November 2025 on Base, a cheaper, faster network built on top of Ethereum by the crypto exchange Coinbase. Networks like Base are called layer 2s because they handle transactions on their own and then report back to Ethereum, the main “layer 1” chain. On October 19, JPMorgan said JPM Coin is now live on Ethereum itself, so clients can move it between both networks. News: JPM Coin (JPMD), @jpmorgan’s USD deposit token, is now live on @ethereum. JPMD extends from Base to Ethereum L1, giving institutional clients native onchain cash that sits alongside the assets, collateral and counterparties they transact with already. J.P. Morgan has now added a cash leg to the products it already live on Ethereum mainnet, with tokenized money market funds MONY and JLTXX both already on the network. — Ethereum Institutional (@ethereuminsti) October 19, 2026 Who’s it for? Crypto firms that need to pay each other on a blockchain, and financial firms that want to settle trades or back tokenized assets, meaning stocks, bonds, or funds recorded as tokens on a blockchain. “Tokenized financial infrastructure is no longer theoretical,” said Emma Landriault, global head of Kinexys Labs. She called the move a step toward “multi-chain optionality,” which means letting clients use the same digital dollars on more than one blockchain. This is the part most coverage skips, and it’s the key to the whole story. A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to always equal $1. Companies like Tether (USDT) and Circle (USDC) issue them and back each one with reserves, mostly cash and short-term US government debt. Stablecoins move freely on public blockchains, and almost anyone can hold them. A deposit token is different. It’s your bank balance, turned into a token. The money never leaves the bank. The token is just a new way to move it. So even though JPM Coin now runs on a public blockchain, it’s permissioned: JPMorgan decides who can send and receive it. Think of it like a private lane on a public highway. Everyone can see the road, but only cars with a pass can use the lane. For years, JPMorgan ran its blockchain projects on private networks it controlled. So why move to Ethereum now? J.P. Morgan now has three tokenized products live on Ethereum mainnet. → JPMD, the USD deposit token, on Ethereum and Base → MONY, tokenized money market fund → JLTXX, tokenized money market fund “Ethereum’s established depth of onchain liquidity and tokenized assets makes it a natural next public blockchain for JPM Coin. Institutional clients can now move money quickly, easily and securely on Ethereum in addition to Base, the Ethereum Layer 2 blockchain… JPM Coin joins a growing set of J.P. Morgan tokenized offerings on Ethereum…” — Ethereum Institutional (@ethereuminsti) October 19, 2026 Because that’s where the money and the customers already are. This also isn’t JPMorgan’s only bet. In January, it said it would bring JPM Coin to the Canton Network, a blockchain built for financial institutions. Having JPM Coin on Base, Ethereum, and soon Canton means JPMorgan wants its digital dollars to work wherever its clients’ assets live. Let’s keep this in proportion. Kinexys processes more than $7 billion a day and over $4 trillion since it started. That sounds huge, until you compare it with JPMorgan’s overall payments business, which moves about $12 trillion a day. By our math, Kinexys handles roughly 0.06% of what the bank moves every day. JPM Coin is a slice of that. So no, JPMorgan isn’t moving the world’s money onto Ethereum. But the direction matters more than the size. The biggest US bank is now comfortable putting its own dollars on the same public network as crypto apps and stablecoins. Five years ago, that would have been unthinkable. Here’s why we think this launch matters beyond JPMorgan. Stablecoins have grown into a market worth about $308 billion, led by Tether’s USDT at roughly $184 billion and Circle’s USDC at about $74 billion. Every dollar that sits in a stablecoin is a dollar that isn’t sitting in a bank. Banks use deposits to fund loans, so losing them hurts. Timing matters too. The GENIUS Act, the new US law setting rules for stablecoins, takes effect on January 18, 2027. Once stablecoin issuers face bank-like rules, the difference between a well-regulated stablecoin and a bank deposit token gets smaller, and the competition gets sharper. The Clarity Act, which aimed to set rules for crypto markets, failed in the Senate in 2026. That leaves the GENIUS Act’s stablecoin rules as the main new crypto law taking effect in 2027. Yes. Issuers like Tether and Circle can freeze tokens at specific addresses, often after hacks. After the Bitget exploit, they froze $318,000 linked to the hack, a small share of the $387 million stolen. Yes, at a growing scale. AI agents have made 138 million crypto payments, mostly in stablecoins, because they settle instantly and work without a bank account. Bitmine is the largest corporate holder of Ether, but its buying has slowed. Some analysts now think Bitmine could start selling ETH, which would matter more for Ether’s price than JPM Coin. Networks built on top of Ethereum bundle many transactions together, which cuts costs. More than 65 leaders represent established companies averaging over $8.6M in annual revenue and collectively employing more than 2,300 nationwide NEW YORK, October 22, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--The D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families (IVMF) at Syracuse University and J.P. Morgan Commercial Banking today announced the 2027 cohort of CEOcircle, bringing together more than 65 veteran and military spouse business leaders running established companies across the country. Companies entering this year's cohort average $8.6 million in annual revenue and collectively employ more than 2,300 individuals. Participants represent industries including technology, government contracting and manufacturing, demonstrating the scale and reach of veteran and military spouse-led companies operating across the U.S. economy. The 2027 cohort marks the latest chapter in a relationship between JPMorganChase and D'Aniello IVMF that spans more than 15 years. That work has grown alongside the military-connected businesses it serves, creating programming for entrepreneurs at different stages of business ownership. CEOcircle, launched in collaboration with J.P. Morgan Commercial Banking in 2021, was built specifically for established veteran and military spouse business leaders navigating the demands of continued growth. CEOcircle is a yearlong peer accountability training program tailored to help mid-size veteran and military spouse executives scale their businesses. Since 2021, more than 250 business leaders have participated in the program. "Supporting veteran and military spouse business leaders is about creating opportunity and strengthening communities," said U.S. Air Force Veteran Alex McKindra, Managing Director in Global Corporate Banking and Head of Global Banking Veteran Initiatives at J.P. Morgan. "CEOcircle brings together leaders who are committed to learning from one another, growing their businesses and creating jobs across the country. We're proud to work with D'Aniello IVMF to help foster the connections that enable their continued success." "We are proud to welcome an exceptional new cohort of veteran and military spouse entrepreneurs to CEOcircle: accomplished leaders who are building successful companies, creating jobs and contributing to economic growth nationwide," said U.S. Army Veteran Ray Toenniessen, Executive Director of D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families. "CEOcircle provides a community of peers, strategic connections and business expertise to equip entrepreneurs for their next phase of growth. Together with J.P. Morgan, we are building on more than 15 years of partnership and a shared commitment to creating opportunities for veteran and military spouse entrepreneurs to achieve sustained success." The majority of graduating CEOcircle participants report gaining new business opportunities through their experience. The network also extends beyond the yearlong program, with alumni continuing to participate in dedicated events, returning for additional programming and serving as facilitators for future cohorts. CEOcircle sits at the most advanced stage of IVMF's entrepreneurship continuum, which connects military-connected entrepreneurs with programming and resources from business ideation through startup, growth and established-company leadership. D'Aniello IVMF's broader entrepreneurship community now includes more than 100,000 veteran and military spouse entrepreneurs nationwide. The full list of companies selected to participate in the 2027 CEOcircle cohort is available on IVMF's website. Companies interested in participating in the next CEOcircle program, or other programs IVMF leads for veteran and military spouse owned businesses, can learn more here. To learn more about how J.P. Morgan Commercial Banking supports U.S. veterans and military spouses in business, their families and the broader military community, explore the firm's website here. Through programs in career training, entrepreneurship, community services and research, D'Aniello IVMF advances opportunity across the military-connected community. title: Finding opportunities in Asia equities amid the selloff - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. After a powerful run in AI and technology equities, October has delivered a sharp reminder that winning investments rarely move in a straight line. Semiconductors – which have been leading for most of the AI rally – saw a sharp selloff as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index posted one of its longest losing streaks since 2008. It fell eight consecutive sessions through mid-October to and currently trades at 20% off year-to-date peaks. Closely-related tech-heavy markets in Asia such as Taiwan and Korea are also down by around 10% and 30% from peak levels respectively. The catalysts are familiar. There seems to be a constant flow doubt over the AI story. From uncertainties over Anthropic’s near-term revenue trajectory reigniting debates over the economics of the AI buildout, neocloud credit availability questioning 2028 capex assumptions, to headlines around data-center project delays and intensifying voter and political opposition ahead of the midterm elections – many factors have added to market volatility. Some questions are dominating client conversations: Is the AI capex cycle sustainable, or are we approaching a top? Are valuations in AI winners stretched to the point where the risk-reward is no longer attractive? How should investors think about near-term technical pressures such as narrow market leadership, concentration within indices and financing concerns as rates rise? Some Asian markets have been core to the AI buildout and have delivered market-leading returns – but are most of the returns behind us? As we stand at the start of the fourth quarter, this has broadly been a positive year of equity returns in aggregate for Asia despite the recent selloff. However, there has also been large divergence in equity returns, with Korea and Taiwan delivering around 60% returns YTD (USD terms) while China's Offshore and India's equity markets have declined by around 15%. Similar to the US, parts of Asia have been undergoing an earnings super-cycle due to the ongoing AI infrastructure buildout, and this is one key reason driving a divergence in earnings revisions so far this year. Investors have rewarded markets with earnings upside, while rightfully penalizing those with weaker earnings outlooks. In this week’s Asia Strategy Focus, we dive deeper into the earnings progress across the Asian equities landscape in the first nine months of 2026, and detail our thoughts and investment outlook going forward. Starting with Korea, due to the ongoing memory shortage as AI demand outstrips supply, earnings expectations for 2026/2027 have seen an incredible 183%/243% positive revision since the beginning of the year. This has been the driving force for the impressive market returns year-to-date. Understandably, investors are questioning the sustainability of these earnings, and the valuation multiple for Korea has declined by over 50% to just a 4x forward P/E. We came into the year positive on Korean equities, and this remains one of our preferred regions. We continue to be of the view that memory supply and demand will likely stay tight at least into 2028 and potentially beyond. The risk/reward skews positively at this juncture in the markets after the significant near-term pullback. Similarly, Taiwan has been the key manufacturer of leading-edge logic chips that are used for training and inferencing in the rapid adoption of AI across the world. With semiconductors and tech hardware representing 86% of the MSCI Taiwan Index, it provides direct exposure and is a clear beneficiary across the entire AI supply chain. This has driven positive earnings revisions of 38%/53% for 2026/2027 and has been the key driver of Taiwan's above-market returns in 2026. With our current expectations for 2026/2027 earnings to grow by 69%/33%, we view Taiwan's valuation at 18x forward P/E as attractive and continue to recommend the region. Taiwan, alongside Korea, remains some of the cleanest expressions of the global AI hardware theme and sits at the heart of our preferred Asia equity positioning. There have also been notable detractors in Asia equity markets – both Offshore China and Onshore China's equity performance so far this year has been underwhelming. With the domestic economy showing continued signs of slowing down, local governments prioritizing fiscal consolidation, a stronger currency, and heavy AI capital expenditure weighing on reported earnings, this has translated into 2026/2027 consensus expectations declining by 6%/5% through September this year. We have been tactical with Offshore China equities this year and lowered our recommendation at the end of August to neutral given these growing headwinds. We currently expect earnings growth in 2026/2027 of 9%/12%, and with a valuation at 10x forward P/E, we do not find Offshore China compelling and retain our neutral view. We continue to monitor policy support, AI localization progress – where local chips are expected to meet 80% of China's AI infrastructure demand by 2028 – and the pace of internet-platform monetization as potential catalysts for a more constructive stance. Many of the macro headwinds this year, including higher oil prices, a stronger US dollar, and rising global interest rates, have been challenges for the Indian equity market. With the added concern of AI disruption risk for labor outsourcing businesses such as call centers and IT consulting, it is unsurprising that the Indian equity market has underperformed. This is apparent in earnings, which have seen negative revisions of -3.5% in 2027. We have also witnessed a de-rating in the premium valuation that Indian equities have historically commanded relative to Asian equities, as earnings growth is currently less impressive compared to other Asian regions. With an expected earnings growth in 2027/2028 of just 7%/11% and a valuation at 18.4x forward P/E, we do not find the risk/reward attractive and keep our neutral rating. Longer-term structural themes – including physical AI, electronics manufacturing, defense, and a power grid buildout – remain compelling, but the near-term earnings profile does not yet justify a more constructive stance. Similar to developed markets such as the US and Europe, Japan has seen exceptionally strong earnings revisions this year, with 2026/2027 estimates now 16%/14% higher than at the beginning of 2026, and this has driven the TOPIX higher by 17% year-to-date. While technology has benefited from the AI infrastructure buildout, there has also been broad strength across other sectors such as industrials and financials, where rate hikes from the Bank of Japan rate have been particularly impactful. While we hold a positive view on the earnings growth outlook for Japan at 25%/8% in 2026/2027, we find valuations at a forward P/E of 16x mildly high relative to history. We retain a neutral view on Japan and await a better entry point before turning more decidedly positive. In the next couple of weeks, markets are receiving earnings results from the large US hyperscalers and semiconductor supply chain companies, and the midterm elections will be concluded, which could remove some of the uncertainties and overhangs in the market at the moment. Looking further ahead, as we put forth in a previous report on Emerging Markets, EM is no longer just a tactical trade on low valuations – it is increasingly a strategic allocation to the industries the world now needs most: semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical commodities, and AI infrastructure. Asia sits at the core of that case. Taiwan and Korea offer direct beta to global AI compute through the hardware and memory supply chains, while China provides selective exposure to AI localization and platforms. For investors seeking to express the theme more broadly, thematic strategies spanning the AI value chain and EM equity managers can complement single-country exposure. Our message to investors is to stay allocated to AI and tech as the capex cycle, earnings trajectory, and supply-demand backdrop remain intact. We view the current volatility as an opportunity to add high-conviction exposure on weakness rather than a reason to retreat. However, right-sizing those allocations is key. The concentration risk is real: Korea and Taiwan already represent more than half of the MSCI EM (Emerging Markets) Index, and significant overweights could leave portfolios heavily dependent on a single theme. Pair conviction AI exposure with uncorrelated sources of return, and maintain diversification across regions and asset classes. The recent market volatility is uncomfortable, but it is the price of admission to one of the most important investment themes of this decade. Our conviction remains unchanged – and the dispersion within Asia offers a rich opportunity set.
